1.goal: To name the scene: it is the Meteoro meeting, with the automatic translation switched on.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is accepted here.
run: Ask when the last meeting was and what she did there. One answer, then move.
Say this once: today is not about understanding everything. It is about ASKING, one time.
exact: Today is not about understanding everything. It is about asking, one time.
1.expected: One concrete meeting, most likely one she sat through in silence.
1.support: If nothing comes, ask what she does when the meeting is in English and she has the translation on.
1.challenge: Ask what she would have wanted to ask in that meeting, and what stopped her.
1.monitoring: Whether she names silence as the problem, or comprehension. Today's object is the first.
1.evidence: The meeting she names — it is the scene the lesson gives back.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example.

2.goal: Who the two are, and why she is listening.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the card on screen together.
run: Read the card with her.
Confirm: they are two people she has never met, and each one speaks for thirty seconds.
Do not give away any of the four pieces of information. The prediction depends on it.
2.expected: That she knows she is about to hear two introductions and nothing else.
2.support: If the setting stays vague, ask what she would want to know about each of them afterwards.
2.challenge: Ask which of the two she would rather speak to first.
2.monitoring: Whether she is already trying to predict the content. Hold it for the next screen.
2.evidence: Whether she can say what she is about to hear.
2.transition: Move on when she knows what she is going to hear.

3.goal: To risk what an introduction contains, before hearing one.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions. Guesses, not answers.
run: Read the three questions OUT LOUD WITH her.
Accept any guess; do not confirm and do not correct.
If she will not risk one, offer two options and ask her to choose.
exact: The two options: “Do they always say their name, or only what they do?”
After the guess, without confirming: “Good. That is your guess. Let us listen.”
3.expected: Three guesses, however tentative. Name, role, place and reason are the usual four.
3.support: If she will not commit, offer the two options and let her pick one. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask which of the four she would say first if it were her turn.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess at all. It is the habit the block works on.
3.evidence: The four things she predicts — they are what she listens for.
3.transition: Move on when she has risked all three.

4.goal: To hear both introductions once, with no transcript, only for the two questions on screen.
4.interaction: S listens to both in a row, then T–S.
run: The questions are already on screen — read them WITH her before you press play.
Play the two introductions one after the other.
DO NOT OPEN THE TRANSCRIPT. She will ask. It opens at stage 5.
exact: How many people spoke? (Two.) Did either of them ask you anything? (No.)
4.support: Replay before slowing down. Slowing helps only when speed itself is the blocker.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two was easier to follow, and why.
4.monitoring: Whether she listens for the two questions or tries to catch everything. Catching everything is what she does today and it does not work.
4.evidence: What one listening gives her without support. The first listening measure of the cycle.
4.transition: Move on when she answers both, even partially.

5.goal: To attribute each piece of information to whoever said it — and to find the one nobody said.
5.interaction: S classifies; you stop the audio where she loses it. Transcript available.
run: Play again, stopping where she loses it. Now the transcript may open.
exact: Who is in the group for the first time? (Marta.)
5.expected: Six items attributed, with one of them said by nobody.
5.support: If an item resists, replay only the ten seconds it depends on and ask who is speaking.
5.challenge: Ask what she would have to ask to find out the one nobody said.
5.monitoring: The item that decides: “has two children” is NOT in the audio. If she marks it as said, she is filling a gap with an assumption — and it is worth naming, gently.
5.evidence: Whether she fills gaps with assumptions. It comes back in every meeting she sits in.
5.transition: Move on when the six are checked.

6.goal: For HER to formulate what separates a request that works from one that does not.
6.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S until she words it herself.
run: Four lines on screen; she marks the two that recover what was missed.
Then ask what is different about the two she chose.
Accept the wording in Portuguese and give it back in English.
exact: What is different about the two you chose?
6.expected: The answer you want, from her: the two say WHICH piece was missed.
6.support: If the difference will not come, read one of each out loud and ask which one tells the other person where to start again.
6.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the weak ones into a strong one, on the spot.
6.monitoring: Whether she reaches the distinction herself. Handing it over costs the stage.
6.evidence: Her own wording of the difference. It is what stage 7 practices.
6.transition: Move on when she has said the difference.

7.goal: The requests said out loud, at the right moment.
7.interaction: T plays and stops; S produces the request on the spot. Four stopping points.
run: Play again and stop at four points. At each one she produces the request, on the spot.
If she waits for the end, go back and redo the point.
Include a name to spell — “Reyes” — and ask her to use “how do you spell that?” and write it down.
Correction here is immediate and gentle.
7.expected: Four requests, each naming the piece that was missed, plus one spelling request.
7.support: If the request will not come, give the first three words and let her finish.
7.challenge: Stop at a fifth point she did not expect and see whether it still comes.
7.monitoring: Whether the request arrives at the moment of the loss, or after the speaker has finished.
7.evidence: How many of the four come out at the right moment.
7.transition: Move on when the four have come out.

8.goal: The production of the lesson — she introduces herself and asks ONE question, uninvited.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are Marta, who has just introduced herself.
run: Marta has just introduced herself. Now it is her turn: two sentences about herself, and ONE question.
DO NOT INVITE HER TO SPEAK. No “Joice, do you have a question?”. That question does the work that is hers — and it is exactly what does not happen in a real meeting.
Offer the opening (“Where do you…?”) if she freezes, and then wait. The silence is work.
Do not correct during.
Record it. If she asks, it is the first question of hers in English that is on record.
exact: The opening, if she freezes: “Where do you…?”
8.expected: Two sentences of introduction and one question, asked without being invited.
8.support: Offer only the first two or three words. Do not complete the question for her.
8.challenge: Answer with something unexpected and see whether a second question follows.
8.monitoring: Whether the question comes out at all, and whether it comes before you invite it.
8.evidence: The recording, and whether the question happened. It is the first one on record.
8.transition: Move on when the question has come out, or at four minutes.

9.goal: To hand back two points and to ask for one request at a slightly higher speed.
9.interaction: T–S, two short points, then one replay.
run: Two things, short.
Count the questions out loud with her — if one came out, say it is the first in seven lessons. That is a result, and she needs to hear it as one.
Then: the same audio a little faster, one request only, chosen by her.
Do not add new content.
exact: You asked one question. That is the first one in seven lessons. That is the result of today.
9.expected: One request, spent on the piece that mattered.
9.support: If she cannot choose, ask which piece she would need to say her own name back correctly.
9.challenge: Run it once more, faster, with the same single request.
9.monitoring: Which request she spends. It says what she treats as essential.
9.evidence: The number of questions and requests. Both go in the record.
9.transition: Move on when the faster round has been done.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close.
run: She ticks what she recognizes.

Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has the two introductions at full speed with no transcript, and her own introduction written in four sentences — which is what she will say in lesson 12.
Announce lesson 11: the form of the question itself — six questions in a row, each one born from the previous answer.
exact: Next lesson is the question itself — six of them, one after another. That is the part the first eight lessons never asked of you.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, ask which request she would use in the next Meteoro meeting.
10.challenge: Ask when the next meeting is, and which of the four things she will say about herself.
10.monitoring: A low mark after a question that came out is worth recording — it is the gap between doing and knowing that she did.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close. Note whether she formed any question, and how much she understood without the transcript.
